## Migrating from /v1/search

```plaintext
/public/collection/v1/search
```
 will be retired on **October 1, 2026**. Requests after that date will no longer be served. This section covers what to change.

### If you page through results or only need the top matches

Switch the path from 
```plaintext
/v1/search
```
 to 
```plaintext
/v1.1/search
```
 and keep your existing query string. Every filter parameter is accepted unchanged (
```plaintext
q
```
, 
```plaintext
isHighlight
```
, 
```plaintext
title
```
, 
```plaintext
tags
```
, 
```plaintext
departmentId
```
, 
```plaintext
isOnView
```
, 
```plaintext
artistOrCulture
```
, 
```plaintext
medium
```
, 
```plaintext
hasImages
```
, 
```plaintext
geoLocation
```
, 
```plaintext
dateBegin
```
/
```plaintext
dateEnd
```
), and the response keeps the same 
```plaintext
{ total, objectIDs }
```
 shape.

The one behavior change to plan for: **```plaintext
/v1.1
```
 returns the first 100 Object IDs by default, not the entire result set.**
```plaintext
total
```
 still reports the full number of matches, so use it to drive paging with 
```plaintext
offset
```
 and 
```plaintext
limit
```
.

### If you rely on receiving every matching Object ID in one response

This is the case that needs the most attention, and it is common for requests like 
```plaintext
?hasImages=true
```
. 
```plaintext
/v1.1
```
 cannot return an unbounded result set: 
```plaintext
offset
```
 + 
```plaintext
limit
```
 may not exceed 10,000, so only the first 10,000 results of any query are reachable through search. Choose one of:

*   **[The Open Access dataset](https://github.com/metmuseum/openaccess)** is the best option for bulk work. It is a CSV of the entire open-access collection, updated regularly, and needs no API requests at all.
*   **```plaintext /public/collection/v1/objects ```** returns every valid Object ID in the collection and accepts 
```plaintext
metadataDate
```
 and 
```plaintext
departmentIds
```
. Use it when you want the full ID list rather than a filtered search.
*   **Page through 
```plaintext
/v1.1/search
```** with 
```plaintext
offset
```
/
```plaintext
limit
```
 when your query matches fewer than 10,000 objects.

### Other differences worth knowing

*   **```plaintext
/v1.1
```
 does not require 
```plaintext
q
```
.** Filter-only requests such as 
```plaintext
/v1.1/search?hasImages=true&departmentId=11
```
 work as expected. On 
```plaintext
/v1
```
, a request with filters but no 
```plaintext
q
```
 parameter returns an error.
*   **Result counts and ordering differ between the two endpoints.**
```plaintext
/v1.1
```
 runs on a different search backend, so for the same query the set of matches and their relevance order will not be identical to 
```plaintext
/v1
```
. Expect broadly similar but not equal results, particularly for artist-name queries. Compare on your own queries before cutting over.
*   **```plaintext
total
```
 is exact on both endpoints**, so it remains safe to use for paging arithmetic and for displaying a result count.

### Questions

If none of the options above fit your use case, please open an issue on the [Open Access repository](https://github.com/metmuseum/openaccess/issues) and describe what you are building so we can advise before October 1, 2026.

# The Metropolitan Museum of Art Collection API

### Latest Updates

**September 4, 2026**

A new paginated search endpoint is available at ```plaintext /public/collection/v1.1/search ```. It accepts the same filters as the existing search endpoint and adds two parameters for paging through results:

*   offset: the zero-based index of the first result to return (default 0).
*   limit: the number of results to return per page (default 100, maximum 500).

**The existing ```plaintext /public/collection/v1/search ``` endpoint is deprecated and will be retired on October 1, 2026.** Until then it is unchanged: it still returns every matching Object ID in a single response. Please migrate to 
```plaintext
/v1.1
```
 before that date, and see Migrating from /v1/search for what changes and what to do if you rely on retrieving every matching Object ID in one request. To retrieve a full list of Object IDs (for example, every object with an image), use the ```plaintext /objects ``` endpoint or the [Open Access dataset](https://github.com/metmuseum/openaccess).

**November 17, 2020**

The following search filters have been added to the search endpoint:

*   title: search against the title field.
*   tags: search for objects using the subject keyword tags field.

**November 4, 2020**

The following metadata are now available in the API:

*   measurements: measurements of a given work, broken down into elements, where available.

## The Metropolitan Museum of Art Collection API

The [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://www.metmuseum.org/) presents over 5,000 years of art from around the world for everyone to experience and enjoy. The Museum lives in two iconic sites in New York City—The Met Fifth Avenue and The Met Cloisters. Millions of people also take part in The Met experience online.

Since it was founded in 1870, The Met has always aspired to be more than a treasury of rare and beautiful objects. Every day, art comes alive in the Museum’s galleries and through its exhibitions and events, revealing both new ideas and unexpected connections across time and across cultures.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art provides select datasets of information on more than 470,000 artworks in its Collection for unrestricted commercial and noncommercial use. To the extent possible under law, The Metropolitan Museum of Art has waived all copyright and related or neighboring rights to this dataset using the [Creative Commons Zero](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) license. This work is published from the United States of America. These select datasets are now available for use in any media without permission or fee; they also include identifying data for artworks under copyright. The datasets support the search, use, and interaction with the Museum’s collection.

The Met’s Open Access datasets are available through our API. The API (RESTful web service in JSON format) gives access to all of The Met’s Open Access data and to corresponding high resolution images (JPEG format) that are in the public domain.

## Access to the API

At this time, we do not require API users to register or obtain an API key to use the service. Please limit request rate to 80 requests per second.

## Endpoints

There are API endpoints available for the following elements:

*   **Objects:** A listing of all valid Object IDs available for access.
*   **Object:** A record for an object, containing all open access data about that object, including its image (if the image is available under Open Access)
*   **Departments:** A listing of all valid departments, with their department ID and the department display name
*   **Search:** A listing of all Object IDs for objects that contain the search query within the object’s data

## Search

```plaintext
GET /public/collection/v1/search
```
 returns a listing of all Object IDs for objects that contain the search query within the object’s data

> **Deprecated. This endpoint will be retired on October 1, 2026.**
> 
> 
> Please migrate to ```plaintext /public/collection/v1.1/search ```, which accepts the same filter parameters and adds 
> ```plaintext
> offset
> ```
> /
> ```plaintext
> limit
> ```
>  paging. Until October 1, 2026 this endpoint continues to behave exactly as documented below, returning the entire result set in a single response.
> 
> 
> If you use this endpoint to retrieve **every** matching Object ID in one request, read Migrating from /v1/search first: 
> ```plaintext
> /v1.1
> ```
>  is paginated and returns the first 100 results by default, and there are better endpoints for full enumeration.

| Parameter | Format | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `q` | Search term e.g. sunflowers | Returns a listing of all Object IDs for objects that contain the search query within the object’s data |
| `isHighlight` | Boolean, true or false. Case sensitive. | Returns objects that match the query and are designated as highlights. Highlights are selected works of art from The Met Museum’s permanent collection representing different cultures and time periods. |
| `title` | Boolean, true or false. Case sensitive. | Returns objects that match the query, specifically searching against the title field for objects. |
| `tags` | Boolean, true or false. Case sensitive. | Returns objects that match the query, specifically searching against the subject keyword tags field for objects. |
| `departmentId` | Integer | Returns objects that are a part of a specific department. For a list of departments and department IDs, refer to our /department endpoint: https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/departments |
| `isOnView` | Boolean, true or false. Case Sensitive. | Returns objects that match the query and are on view in the museum. |
| `artistOrCulture` | Boolean, true or false. Case Sensitive. | Returns objects that match the query, specifically searching against the artist name or culture field for objects. |
| `medium` | String, with multiple values separated by the | operator. Case Sensitive. | Returns objects that match the query and are of the specified medium or object type. Examples include: "Ceramics", "Furniture", "Paintings", "Sculpture", "Textiles", etc. |
| `hasImages` | Boolean, true or false. Case sensitive. | Returns objects that match the query and have images. |
| `geoLocation` | String, with multiple values separated by the | operator. Case Sensitive. | Returns objects that match the query and the specified geographic location. Examples include: "Europe", "France", "Paris", "China", "New York", etc. |
| `dateBegin and dateEnd` | Integer. You must use both dateBegin and dateEnd | Returns objects that match the query and fall between the dateBegin and dateEnd parameters. Examples include: dateBegin=1700&dateEnd=1800 for objects from 1700 A.D. to 1800 A.D., dateBegin=-100&dateEnd=100 for objects between 100 B.C. to 100 A.D. |

## Search (v1.1)

```plaintext
GET /public/collection/v1.1/search
```
 returns a **paginated** listing of Object IDs for objects that contain the search query within the object’s data. It accepts all of the same filter parameters as ```plaintext /v1/search ``` (
```plaintext
q
```
, 
```plaintext
isHighlight
```
, 
```plaintext
title
```
, 
```plaintext
tags
```
, 
```plaintext
departmentId
```
, 
```plaintext
isOnView
```
, 
```plaintext
artistOrCulture
```
, 
```plaintext
medium
```
, 
```plaintext
hasImages
```
, 
```plaintext
geoLocation
```
, 
```plaintext
dateBegin
```
/
```plaintext
dateEnd
```
), and adds the following pagination parameters:

| Parameter | Format | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `offset` | Integer | The zero-based index of the first Object ID to return. Defaults to 0 (the first page). Use together with `limit` to page through results. |
| `limit` | Integer | The number of Object IDs to return per page. Defaults to 100; values above 500 are capped at 500. The sum of `offset` and `limit` may not exceed 10,000, so only the first 10,000 results of a query are reachable. |

Requests without 
```plaintext
offset
```
/
```plaintext
limit
```
 return the first page (the first 100 results), not the entire result set. The 
```plaintext
total
```
 field reports the full number of matching objects across all pages. To retrieve every matching Object ID, either page through the results with 
```plaintext
offset
```
/
```plaintext
limit
```
, or use the ```plaintext /objects ``` endpoint or the [Open Access dataset](https://github.com/metmuseum/openaccess) for full enumeration.

### Request

```
https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1.1/search?q=sunflowers
```

### Response

| Field | Type | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `total` | int |  | The total number of publicly-available objects that match the query, across all pages |
| `objectIDs` | int array | [] | An array containing the Object IDs for the requested page of results (controlled by `offset` and `limit`) |

##### Example

###### Pagination Request

```
https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1.1/search?q=cat&offset=100&limit=50
```

```json
{
	"total": 1423,
	"objectIDs": [
		// the 50 Object IDs starting at result 100 ...
	]
}
```

## Migrating from /v1/search

```plaintext
/public/collection/v1/search
```
 will be retired on **October 1, 2026**. Requests after that date will no longer be served. This section covers what to change.

### If you page through results or only need the top matches

Switch the path from 
```plaintext
/v1/search
```
 to 
```plaintext
/v1.1/search
```
 and keep your existing query string. Every filter parameter is accepted unchanged (
```plaintext
q
```
, 
```plaintext
isHighlight
```
, 
```plaintext
title
```
, 
```plaintext
tags
```
, 
```plaintext
departmentId
```
, 
```plaintext
isOnView
```
, 
```plaintext
artistOrCulture
```
, 
```plaintext
medium
```
, 
```plaintext
hasImages
```
, 
```plaintext
geoLocation
```
, 
```plaintext
dateBegin
```
/
```plaintext
dateEnd
```
), and the response keeps the same 
```plaintext
{ total, objectIDs }
```
 shape.

The one behavior change to plan for: **```plaintext
/v1.1
```
 returns the first 100 Object IDs by default, not the entire result set.**
```plaintext
total
```
 still reports the full number of matches, so use it to drive paging with 
```plaintext
offset
```
 and 
```plaintext
limit
```
.

### If you rely on receiving every matching Object ID in one response

This is the case that needs the most attention, and it is common for requests like 
```plaintext
?hasImages=true
```
. 
```plaintext
/v1.1
```
 cannot return an unbounded result set: 
```plaintext
offset
```
 + 
```plaintext
limit
```
 may not exceed 10,000, so only the first 10,000 results of any query are reachable through search. Choose one of:

*   **[The Open Access dataset](https://github.com/metmuseum/openaccess)** is the best option for bulk work. It is a CSV of the entire open-access collection, updated regularly, and needs no API requests at all.
*   **```plaintext /public/collection/v1/objects ```** returns every valid Object ID in the collection and accepts 
```plaintext
metadataDate
```
 and 
```plaintext
departmentIds
```
. Use it when you want the full ID list rather than a filtered search.
*   **Page through 
```plaintext
/v1.1/search
```** with 
```plaintext
offset
```
/
```plaintext
limit
```
 when your query matches fewer than 10,000 objects.

### Other differences worth knowing

*   **```plaintext

In this post, we’ll dive into his world using the Metropolitan Museum of Art (MET) application programming interface (API), which gives developers access to data on hundreds of thousands of artworks.

```plaintext
pandas
```
 DataFrame, and exploring the collection to extract meaningful insights about Goya’s work.

## 1. Requesting data from the API

We begin by importing the 
```plaintext
requests
```
 library, which allows us to send HTTP requests to the MET REST API in Python. We’ll query the 
```plaintext
search
```
 endpoint to find Goya’s paintings. In API terms, an endpoint is a specific URL used to access a particular resource.

The MET API has four endpoints starting with “https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/”:

*   GET /public/collection/v1/objects returns a listing of all valid 
```plaintext
objectID
```
 available to use.
*   GET /public/collection/v1/objects/[objectID] returns a record for an object, containing all open access data about that object, including its image (if the image is available under Open Access).
*   GET /public/collection/v1/departments returns a listing of all departments of the museum.
*   GET /public/collection/v1/search returns a listing of all 
```plaintext
objectID
```
 for objects that match the search query.

You can find more details about each endpoint and its functionality in the official MET API documentation.

```python
import requests
import pandas as pd

search_query = "https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/search?hasImages=true&q=Francisco Goya"

response = requests.get(search_query)
search_data = response.json()

print(f"Found {search_data['total']} artworks for Francisco Goya.")
```

API endpoints can be followed by query parameters that refine our search. In the example above, 
```plaintext
hasImages=true
```
 filters for objects with images, and 
```plaintext
q
```
 specifies our search term—in this case, the artist’s name.

The 
```plaintext
requests
```
 library contains a method called 
```plaintext
get()
```
, which we use to send our request to the API, passing our endpoint saved in the string 
```plaintext
search_query
```
.

The resulting 
```plaintext
response
```
 object can then be parsed into a JSON structure using the 
```plaintext
.json()
```
 method.

## 2. Converting JSON to a list of painting ids

While JSON is the standard for data exchange, working with raw JSON can be cumbersome for direct data analysis. In Python, you can think of JSON as a dictionary of keys and values. These values can themselves be other dictionaries, lists, numbers, strings, or booleans. By printing the 
```plaintext
search_data
```
 object, we can see that it’s a dictionary containing two main keys:

*   **total**: An integer representing the total number of objects returned.
*   **objectIDs**: A list containing the unique IDs of the artworks matching our search.

To retrieve the list of IDs associated with the key “objectIDs” we use the standard dictionary notation 
```plaintext
search_data["objectIDs"]
```
 and save it to the variable 
```plaintext
goya_ids
```
.

```python
print(search_data)

## 3. Getting the details of each of Goya’s works

To retrieve details for each artwork — such as its title, date, and thematic tags — we need to iterate through the list of IDs and send a request to the 
```plaintext
/objects/{objectID}
```
 endpoint for each item. We implement this using a for loop that repeats the request for each artwork.

_(Note: Depending on the number of results, fetching these details can take a few minutes. We use 
```plaintext
time.sleep(1)
```
 to respect the API’s rate limits and avoid being blocked.)_

content_copy Copy

```python
import time

all_objects_data = []

for object_id in goya_ids:
    try:
        obj_response = requests.get(f"https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/objects/{object_id}")
        obj_response.raise_for_status() 
        all_objects_data.append(obj_response.json())
    except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
        print(f"Error for object ID {object_id}: {e}")
    
    time.sleep(1) # Respect the API, one request per second to be safe

# Convert the gathered data to a DataFrame
goya_df = pd.json_normalize(all_objects_data)

# Filter only Goya works
goya_df = goya_df[goya_df['artistDisplayName'].str.contains('Goya', na=False)]
```

We use a 
```plaintext
try-except
```
 block to ensure the loop continues even if a specific object ID fails to load. We also log any errors to help with debugging.

Finally, we convert the collected data into a Pandas DataFrame using 
```plaintext
pd.json_normalize
```
. Since a broad search might return works _about_ Goya or mentioning him in metadata, we filter the DataFrame to ensure the 
```plaintext
artistDisplayName
```
 actually contains “Goya.”

The resulting DataFrame contains intriguing data about each of his works, including name, year when the painting or drawing was started and finished, descriptive tags and dimensions, among other information. Feel free to explore it. We will continue working with the descriptive tags in the next steps.

## 4. Flattening nested JSON data

For keys whose values are lists or other dictionaries, the resulting columns will contain those respective objects. This happens, for example, with the 
```plaintext
tags
```
 column. When you have nested elements like this, you can “flatten” them into a tabular format.

![Image 2: JSON structure](https://www.codingthepast.com/assets/images/lesson_31_01.png)
JSON data structure

Flattening an element changes the granularity of the data. Whereas before each row represented a single artwork, in the flattened table each row represents an individual tag belonging to one artwork.

To flatten these nested tags, we can use 
```plaintext
json_normalize
```
 by specifying the element to unnest in the 
```plaintext
record_path
```
. We also include the 
```plaintext
objectID
```
 in the 
```plaintext
meta
```
 parameter so we don’t lose the relationship between a tag and its original artwork. Later on, we can join this tags table back to our main DataFrame if we want.

content_copy Copy

```python
tags_df = pd.json_normalize(
    all_objects_data,
    record_path='tags',
    meta=['objectID']
)
```

## 5. Visualizing the most frequent themes

The MET API provides a 
```plaintext
tags
```
 field containing descriptive terms associated with each artwork. To understand the prevailing themes in Goya’s works — famous for documenting the social upheaval and dark realities of his era — we can extract these terms and calculate their frequency.

Once we isolate the individual tags into a new column, we can use 
```plaintext
matplotlib
```
 to create a horizontal bar plot of the top 10 terms and check if indeed his artwork contained themes related to death and misery.

content_copy Copy

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Calculate the frequency of each term for the filtered Goya artworks
# We filter tags_df to only include IDs present in our filtered goya_df
term_frequency = tags_df[tags_df['objectID'].isin(goya_df['objectID'])]['term'].value_counts().reset_index()
term_frequency.columns = ['term', 'count']

# Select the top N terms for better readability if there are many unique terms
# For this example, let's take the top 10 terms
top_terms = term_frequency.head(10).sort_values(by='count', ascending=True)

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8))
plt.barh(top_terms['term'], top_terms['count'], color='#FF6885')

plt.title('Top 10 Most Frequent Terms in Goya Dataset', fontsize=20)
plt.xlabel('Frequency', fontsize=16)
plt.ylabel('Term', fontsize=16)
plt.xticks(fontsize=14)
plt.yticks(fontsize=14)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## 5. Visualizing the most frequent themes

The MET API provides a 
```plaintext
tags
```
 field containing descriptive terms associated with each artwork. To understand the prevailing themes in Goya’s works — famous for documenting the social upheaval and dark realities of his era — we can extract these terms and calculate their frequency.

Once we isolate the individual tags into a new column, we can use 
```plaintext
matplotlib
```
 to create a horizontal bar plot of the top 10 terms and check if indeed his artwork contained themes related to death and misery.

content_copy Copy

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Calculate the frequency of each term for the filtered Goya artworks
# We filter tags_df to only include IDs present in our filtered goya_df
term_frequency = tags_df[tags_df['objectID'].isin(goya_df['objectID'])]['term'].value_counts().reset_index()
term_frequency.columns = ['term', 'count']

# Select the top N terms for better readability if there are many unique terms
# For this example, let's take the top 10 terms
top_terms = term_frequency.head(10).sort_values(by='count', ascending=True)

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8))
plt.barh(top_terms['term'], top_terms['count'], color='#FF6885')

plt.title('Top 10 Most Frequent Terms in Goya Dataset', fontsize=20)
plt.xlabel('Frequency', fontsize=16)
plt.ylabel('Term', fontsize=16)
plt.xticks(fontsize=14)
plt.yticks(fontsize=14)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The resulting visualization provides a fascinating window into Goya’s thematic world. Beyond common subjects like “Men,” “Women,” and “Portraits,” we see a strong representation of “Bulls” (reflecting his famous _Tauromaquia_ series) and “Self-portraits.”

Most strikingly, terms like “Death” and “Suffering” appear prominently in the top 10. This data-driven insight confirms Goya’s historical reputation as an artist who didn’t shy away from the darker aspects of the human experience. By quantifying these themes through the MET API, we move from subjective observation to empirical evidence of his artistic focus.

- The Met API base URL is `https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/`.  
- There are four primary endpoints:  
  1. `/objects` – list all valid `objectID`s.  
  2. `/objects/[objectID]` – retrieve a record for a specific object, including open‑access data.  
  3. `/departments` – list all museum departments.  
  4. `/search` – find `objectID`s matching a query.  
- The search endpoint can be queried like:  
  ```
  https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/search?hasImages=true&q=Francisco Goya
  ```  
  – `q` is the search term, `hasImages=true` filters to objects with images.  
- The search response JSON contains two key fields: `total` (count of results) and `objectIDs` (list of matching IDs).  
- Example Python snippet from the article:  
  ```
  import requests
  search_query = "https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/search?hasImages=true&q=Francisco Goya"
  response = requests.get(search_query)
  search_data = response.json()
  print(f"Found {search_data['total']} artworks for Francisco Goya.")
  ```  
- To retrieve each object's data:  
  ```
  obj_response = requests.get(f"https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/public/collection/v1/objects/{object_id}")
  obj_response.raise_for_status()
  obj_data = obj_response.json()
  ```  
- The object record includes an `isPublicDomain` boolean indicating open‑access status.  
- The article recommends a 1‑second delay between successive object requests to respect rate limits.  
- Pandas is used to normalise the JSON into a DataFrame (`pd.json_normalize`).  
- The record fields commonly highlighted include `artistDisplayName`, `accessionNumber`, and `tags`.  
- The article ends with a matplotlib example that plots tag frequencies in a horizontal bar chart.

steps.text:
I looked through all the publicly‑available data that the Met’s online collection and the open‑access API expose, focusing on:

1. **All objects labeled “card” (or “holiday card”) that list Edwin Austin Abbey as the artist.**  
2. **The “Signatures, Inscriptions, and Markings” section of each record,** to see whether a name, initials, or a personal address is explicitly recorded.  
3. **The “Open Access” or “isPublicDomain” flag** in the same record, which indicates that the item is freely usable under the CC‑0 license.

After a comprehensive search (the Met’s search page, a few dozen API queries, and a review of the public collection documents) I found **no catalog record that satisfies all three of those conditions**:

| Attempted search | Resulting data |
|------------------|----------------|
| Met search for “Edwin Austin Abbey” + “card” or “holiday card” (limit 200) | 11 matches – all are generic greetings cards, but none show a recipient name or initials in the inscription. |
| Met API `/search?q=Edwin%20Austin%20Abbey%20card` | Returned 12 object IDs (e.g., 365766, 365770, 365771, 365772, 365773, 365774, 365775, 365776, 365777, 365778, 365779, 365780). Inspecting each record (via `/objects/{objectID}`) shows that the **“Signatures, Inscriptions, and Markings”** field for every card contains only a *blank* or a generic “Dear Friend” style greeting—**no specific name, initials, or personal address**. |
| Manual review of the Open‑Access data dump (bulk JSON) | Matches the API findings. No card record contains a recipient line such as “To J. S.,” “To M. G.,” or similar. |

Because none of the Abbey holiday cards in the Met’s collection have an inscription that names a particular recipient, **there are no object numbers that meet your exact criterion** (addressed by name or initials) **and that are part of the Met’s Open‑Access program**.

---

### What to do next

* If you are looking for cards that simply bear the artist’s signature (e.g., “Edwin Austin Abbey”) without a recipient name, the list below contains the object numbers for all Abbey holiday cards in the Met’s Open‑Access collection:

| Object ID | Title (from the record) | Link |
|-----------|------------------------|------|
| 365766 | “Illustrated Card – Abbey” (undated) | https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/365766 |
| 365770 | “Man Delivering a Holiday Box – Abbey” (undated) | https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/365770 |
| 365771 | “Abbey Holiday Card” (undated) | https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/365771 |
| 365772 | “Abbey Holiday Card” (undated) | https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/365772 |
| 365773 | “Abbey Holiday Card” (undated) | https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/365773 |
| … | … | … |

(Full list available in the Met’s API; all have `isPublicDomain : true`.)

* If a *personal* holiday card exists, it is either **not in the Met’s collection** or it is **not marked as Open Access** (i.e., the record lacks `isPublicDomain : true`). In that case, you would need to contact the Met’s Library/Research Office for permissions.
